skills.name: Two Euclidean pulse generators per track combined with Boolean logic (OR, XOR, AND, SUB), per-generator rotation and whole-track rotation, then printed to an ordinary step sequence for hand edits; also used to redistribute an existing bassline and to leave gaps an arpeggiator fills
skills.goal: Generate musically coherent, non-obvious drum and melodic patterns by combining two Euclidean pulse generators on one track. Each generator spreads N pulses as evenly as possible over the track length (e.g. 16 or 32 steps); numbers that do not divide the length (5, 9, 11, 12) give the interesting grooves. Combine the two with a Boolean operator: OR (any pulse plays; overlaps become one note), XOR (overlaps are removed, leaving space), AND (only overlaps play; the number of possible notes is limited by the smaller pulse count) or SUB (generator 1 minus where it overlaps generator 2, a way to carve notes out). Rotate each generator to change their relationship, then rotate the whole track to move the downbeat of the combined pattern. Print the result to a normal step sequence to edit single notes, apply the same Euclidean distribution to a pre-programmed melodic line (notes stay, positions change), randomise the Euclidean settings with a snapshot to return to, and let an arpeggiator with step offsets fill the gaps. Delta beyond our probability/seeded loop skills: the two-generator Boolean combine plus print-to-steps workflow, mapped to Polyrhythm Studio lanes.

skills.name: Endless-accelerando (Risset rhythm) illusion for cinematic tension: the same pattern at double speed fading out and at half speed fading in while tempo automates to double, dropped subdivisions (fade every other note of a six-pulse group as tempo doubles), half-speed (3/4) and third-speed (6/8) copies forming a 3:2 hemiola fractal, voices swapping roles across cycles, and a long note gliding slowly against a sustained pitch
skills.goal: Make a rhythm that seems to speed up forever without ever getting too fast, the rhythmic version of a Shepard tone. Basic form: play a pattern, the same pattern at double speed fading out above it, and at half speed fading in below it, while tempo automates up to double; then loop. In a track: take a group of six steady pulses and, as tempo rises toward double, fade every second note until it disappears, so at double tempo you hear the original rhythm again. Layer the same six-pulse pattern at half speed (three strong pulses, 3/4 feel) and at one-third speed (two pulses, 6/8 feel) for a 3:2 hemiola; give each layer its own dropped-subdivision transformation and fade layers in and out across cycles so the ear never locks onto one, and let a voice that played the 2-pulse role take the 3-pulse role in the next cycle. Double tempo per cycle (150 → 300 → 600 in the video) and reset where the DAW tempo ceiling is reached. Add tension with a long note rising slowly against a sustained pitch, passing every dissonance. Fits Polyrhythm Studio as tempo-scaled lanes with per-lane gain automation.

skills.name: Record a piano for maximum sustain and resonance with a contact/geophone pickup (about 10 Hz–1 kHz) at the most resonant spot plus air microphones inside and above the body for the highs, build a sampler with per-mic blend and a lowpassed 'muffled' mix, then make ambient textures by extreme time-stretching held notes and tails (FFT size: small = grainy, large = smooth; tonal vs noise emphasis) and reuse samples as wavetables, looped dual-sample pads and phaser-hollowed basses
skills.goal: Turn an acoustic piano (or any resonant instrument) into an intimate sample set and ambient source material. Test contact-pickup positions on the body and choose the one that gives the longest, most natural sustain (in the video: the bottom-left corner beside the lowest key; a metal plate inside sounded resonant but metallic). Because the contact pickup captures only about 10 Hz–1 kHz, add air mics: one inside the closed lower body and one on the lid near the keys. Record each note several times, letting it ring fully (low notes 40–50 s), plus the key release. Denoise, align all mics, and build a sampler with a per-mic volume mix; lowpassing the full mix to the contact-pickup range gives a fuller, more sustained muffled piano than the pickup alone. For sound design, extreme-stretch held notes, chords and tiny leftover tails (30 s to over 20 minutes) and adjust FFT size (small = grainy, large = smooth) and tonal-vs-noise emphasis, pitch-shifting results. Reuse samples as wavetables: 16-voice unison with zero phase randomisation, an extreme many-pole phaser with high feedback for hollowness, slow spectral/granular scanning, and two loops of the same note with slightly different loop lengths panned L/R so the beating speeds up at higher pitches.

skills.name: Three rules for making a randomised/Euclidean sequencer sound intentional: constrain (scale, octave range, pitches pulled close, phrase length), repeat (global randomness to zero, reset per-step random, restart points so the phrase retriggers each bar), and simplify (about three pitches, fewer pulses, complexity from layering simple parts), then add hand-made variations on chosen cycles and random pitch options on only the last few notes
skills.goal: Fix a generative patch that sounds aimlessly random. Rule 1, constrain: set a scale (e.g. minor), reduce octave range/voicing, and pull spread-out notes into closer octaves; limit phrase length. Rule 2, repetition creates anticipation: turn global continuous randomisation to zero, reset any per-step randomisation (use only a little, on a couple of notes), and set a restart point so the pitch and trigger lists start together each bar, so the ear can remember the hook. Rule 3, less is more: cut to about three pitches and fewer pulses; get complexity from several simple layers, not one complex one. Then add intentional variation: in a later cycle (e.g. bar 2) add extra notes, copy that variation to other cycles, move start points, push one note up an octave or add a roll; for controlled surprise, give only the last four notes extra pitch options. Apply the same rules to each part. Complements our probability/seeded generative skills as the taming pass.

skills.name: Generative rhythmic sequence from a hand-written 8-step pattern: live length and start-point changes, chance-based rests, a 5-step Euclidean trigger length phasing against the 8 steps (a 40-step cycle), random modulation of octave and scale degree kept subtle, random distortion and release for accents and note lengths, smooth-random slow LFOs on filter and wavetable position, introduced gradually in performance
skills.goal: Turn a short, intentional sequence into an evolving techno or ambient line without writing new notes. Start from a programmed 8-step pattern (or, for pure random, a one-step root note with random → scale degree attenuated to about 7–8 degrees, which gives quantised random melodies within one octave). Vary it by changing pattern length and start point while it plays. Add rests with chance (about 75% means roughly one in four steps silent) and/or a Euclidean trigger length that does not divide the step count (5 against 8): with chance slightly under 100% (about 90%) the 5-step trigger pattern shifts across the 8 notes and the cycle repeats only after 40 steps. Add a tempo-synced delay so echoes fill the rests. Then add pitch variation by patching random to octave (positive for up, negative for down jumps) and to scale degree (jumps of about 4–5 degrees), keeping both subtle so the line's shape survives. Add sound variation: random → distortion (accents) and random → release (note lengths, with a lower base release), and slow smooth-random LFOs (around 5 s) on filter cutoff and wavetable position. Don't use everything at once; bring modulations in gradually across a set.

skills.name: Classic house pad in any synth: minor 9 / minor 7 / major 7 chords, many-voice detuned unison with oscillator retrigger off (free-running), stereo spread from the unison width control or a chorus/ensemble if the synth has none, slightly resonant lowpass plus serial highpass to remove mud, slow LFO on cutoff, slow amp attack with no filter envelope, coloured noise partly bypassing the lowpass, delay + reverb sends; plus a quick pad from a looped chord-stab sample
skills.goal: Build the classic house pad and know which ingredient does what. Use extended chords (minor 9, minor 7, major 7, major 9 and inversions). Turn unison up (up to 16 voices per oscillator, or 32), detune until it is wide and airy but not seasick, and give a second oscillator a different detune so voices do not sit on top of each other. Turn oscillator retrigger off so voices run free; with retrigger on, voices start in phase and just phase against each other. If unison does not spread voices in stereo, use the width control or add a chorus (an ensemble chorus suits pads). Set a lowpass cutoff a little laid-back with some resonance for character, cut the lows with a highpass (in series), and move cutoff with a slow LFO. Use a slow amp attack and full sustain, and remove any filter envelope. Try pulse waves and PWM by LFO, a sub oscillator for weight, and coloured noise at low level fed partly around the lowpass so its highs survive. Finish with delay and reverb sends. Quick alternative: loop a steady section of a chord-stab sample with a crossfade and slow attack, then hide the loop with delay, reverb and a filter.

skills.name: Produce a binaural-beat meditation track: a two-chord pad foundation with long reverb and overlapping glided notes, a sparse echoing piano and subtle bass, volume-automated arrangement, then a binaural layer of two pure sines (440 Hz and 432 Hz for an 8 Hz difference) panned hard left/right, a narrow high-Q EQ cut at the carrier frequency on the music bus so nothing masks it, fades, a gentle limiter (~3 dB input, no audible gain reduction) and WAV/MP3 export at 44.1 kHz
skills.goal: Make the whole track, not just the beat. Start from pads: play a simple two-chord loop (around A and D), add reverb with high decay and wet mix, keep chord changes on the grid, and let notes overlap with glide so transitions slide instead of stepping. Add a short piano line with an echo (more feedback, ping-pong on) and its own reverb, then a subtle low bass on the same roots; pull all levels down to avoid overdrive. Arrange by drawing volume automation so elements enter and leave (less is more; one element can carry minutes), boost the highs with a high shelf on bright parts, put delay before reverb. Binaural layer: a sine at the root frequency (A = 440 Hz) and a duplicate at 432 Hz (8 Hz difference); unpanned they make an audible wobble (monaural beat), panned hard left and right they form the binaural beat. Group the music and cut a narrow notch (high Q) at 440 Hz so the instrumental doesn't overlap the carrier. Fade the beat in and out, keep it quiet but present when muted/unmuted. On the master, add a limiter on the loudest section with only ~3 dB input and no audible gain reduction; export 44.1 kHz WAV plus an MP3, then do a calm test listen later and adjust.

skills.name: Add an isochronic pulse layer under an existing track: a sine (or noise) carrier played by one long MIDI note, amplitude-pulsed at a chosen rate (e.g. 4 Hz) with a smooth-step pulse shape and a 0–100% isochronic blend, faded in and out by gain automation, with the pulse rate automated (e.g. 15 Hz → 4 Hz → 15 Hz) using ~10 ms parameter smoothing, carrier tuned by reference (440/432) or a custom note-to-frequency map and verified with a tuner, then mixed barely audible
skills.goal: Build the Mind Amend-style isochronic layer as its own track. A tone generator plays a sine carrier from MIDI; with beat frequency 0 it is just a plain sine. Pick the pulse rate (e.g. 4 Hz) and raise the isochronic blend from 0% (steady tone) through 50% to 100% (full on/off pulses); choose a smooth-step pulse shape for focused but soft pulses. An amplitude-pulsing (LFO/tremolo) device lets you pulse noise or any audio as well. Use one long MIDI note for an uninterrupted tone (chords also work and pulse together). Fade in over about 30 s and out over 30–60 s with gain automation. Automate the pulse rate with exact typed breakpoints (e.g. start 15 Hz, glide to 4 Hz, return to 15 Hz at the end) and set the device's parameter smoothing to its minimum (0.01 = 10 ms) for automation. Keep pulse rates low (the speaker suggests below ~100 Hz); carrier frequencies (e.g. 432 Hz reference tuning, or a custom mapping where a note equals 528 Hz) are a separate layer of choice; check the actual pitch with a tuner set to the same reference. Finally set the layer's level in the mixer so it sits barely audible under the music. Polyrhythm Studio: OscillatorNode → GainNode whose gain follows a pulse-shaped LFO at rate r(t) with a ramped automation curve.

skills.name: Layered binaural + isochronic track architecture: carrier in the left ear and carrier+beat in the right (e.g. 100/104 or 100/110 Hz), octave-up/down copies for depth, an isochronic pulse ratio-locked to the beat rate (1:1, 1:2, 2:1) with sine pulse shape, optional left-right ping-pong pulsing, extra harmonic/anchor tone layers pulsed at the same rate, a slow lowpass sweep that fades harmonic layers in and out, panned drifting pink/white/brown noise atmosphere, a drone a fifth below, and a 'journey' of timed beat-rate segments with smooth ramps (e.g. 10 → 1.5 Hz descent)
skills.goal: Design richer Mind Amend-style tracks than a bare two-tone beat. Binaural: one pure tone per ear, the right ear tone = carrier + beat (100 Hz left, 104 Hz right gives a 4 Hz beat; removing one ear leaves a steady tone). Isochronic: the same rate as on/off pulsing of a tone; both can play together. Choose any comfortable carrier (100 Hz in the demo, with micro-tuning), add octave layers (½× and 2× carrier) for depth, and pulse layers at a rate locked to the beat by a simple ratio (1:1, half, double) so nothing drifts out of sync when the beat changes; sine pulse shape is preferred. Ping-pong pulse alternates the pulse left/right instead of on/off. Extra harmonic tones (the presenter uses solfeggio-labelled frequencies and says they lack scientific basis) or a fifth/12th harmonic stack are pulsed at the same rate. A lowpass sweep (period ~6 s and longer) fades harmonic layers in and out so no tone is constant. Pink/white/brown noise as wind/ocean air, auto-panned. A low drone a fifth below supports the field. A journey timeline holds a beat rate for set minutes, then glides smoothly to the next (5 Hz 5 min → 2 Hz → 1 Hz; sleep descent 10 → 1.5 Hz; a 12 → 4.5 Hz ramp). Polyrhythm Studio: one shared rate LFO drives beat offset and every pulse lane via integer ratios.

skills.name: Four-source morph engine: an XY/linear crossfade (centre = all four mixed, corners = one source) versus true parameter morphing of analysed (additive + spectral) sources, where the centre is a composite sound, with separate morph positions per element (additive, spectral, pitch, formant, analysed envelope), each driven by its own LFO type
skills.goal: Build evolving hybrid textures from four contrasting sources and know the difference between crossfading and morphing. Crossfade mode only mixes the four sources by an XY point (centre = all four at once, a corner = that source alone) or along X only (A-B, B-C, C-D). Parameter morph needs analysed sources (additive + spectral resynthesis of imported samples, not virtual-analog saws) at a similar pitch; after time alignment, the centre point produces a composite of all four, not a mix. Morph can be split per element: additive partials, spectral processing, pitch, formant and the analysed amplitude envelope of each sample (not the AHDSR), each with its own position. Give each element a different LFO (slow smooth, very fast, stepped) with depth raised, keep a manual centre point, and add reverb. For Polyrhythm Studio: four analysed partial sets interpolated per element by independent control lanes.

skills.name: Use sample-and-hold as a processor on another modulator (not as a random source): step a sine LFO at a rate, automate the LFO rate and the S&H rate separately on a filtered-noise riser so the end seems to slow down through aliasing, and turn a regular step pattern into random hat-loop volume dips with the inverse amount on an FX mix, on a duplicated layer
skills.goal: Delta beyond our random S&H LFO skill: here S&H samples an input modulator at its own rate. With a sine LFO (unipolar, full amount) into the S&H input, a low S&H rate gives coarse steps over the sine and a high rate follows it finely, so you keep the LFO's regularity with random-feeling steps. On white noise through a filter, map S&H → cutoff at a reduced amount; instead of a linear ramp LFO riser over four bars, put the LFO rate and the S&H rate on automation lanes, ramp the LFO rate to maximum and start the S&H rate low (individual steps audible), so near the end the sampled pattern sounds like it is slowing down. For hat loops, feed a random-drawn 4-bar step modulator (1/8 rather than 1/16) into the S&H and map S&H → volume (unipolar, ~80%) for random level dips, map the same S&H inversely to a metallic FX mix, and keep the processed loop as an extra layer over the original.

skills.name: Per-voice, per-parameter random value drawn at each note-on (many synced sample-and-holds): offset compensation for bipolar values at a parameter's minimum or maximum, unison/chord voices that each get different timbre, random envelope times on an arpeggiated FM pluck, per-voice morph between two cloned-then-edited parts, and per-voice random LFO rate with depth brought in by aftertouch
skills.goal: Make every note and every voice differ slightly without sequencing anything. A per-voice random source picks a new value at each key press for each voice the key allocates and for each parameter it modulates (so 8 unison voices get 8 different wavefolder and FM values, and each note in a chord differs). Values are bipolar: if a parameter sits at its minimum, only positive values have an effect, and an open filter only moves when values are negative, so set the base knob to the middle (offset) to use the full range. Good targets: wavefolder, through-zero FM, filter, envelope times on a plucky FM arpeggio (2-octave up/down), filter envelope, and morph between two parts (clone part A to B, edit B, set morph halfway). A global effect at the end of the chain (e.g. ping-pong delay mix or time) cannot vary per voice and takes the highest value. Randomise LFO rate per voice with LFO depth at zero and aftertouch adding depth for expressive control. Maps to Polyrhythm Studio as a per-voice random draw at note-on.

skills.name: Patch three random-gate tools from generic functions: noise sampled-and-held by a clock into a window comparator, ANDed with the clock, as a probability gate skipper (window size = probability); the same with S&H output fed back into the clock rate for free random bursts; and a Bernoulli gate where comparator out and not-out each AND the clock to trigger two panned voices
skills.goal: Make random and probabilistic gates without dedicated modules. Raw noise into a window comparator gives random gates, but only at a very small window size and with no sync or range. Instead, sample-and-hold the noise on a clock and feed the held value to the comparator: keep shift (window position) high so only the top of the held voltage range passes, and use window size as the probability control (max = all pass, fully closed = none). Because the comparator only fires when the window opens, AND its output with the original clock so every clock passes at maximum. For free random bursts, feed the S&H output back into the clock's rate CV for an unsteady clock. For a Bernoulli gate, use the comparator's out and not-out, each ANDed with the clock (a VCA works as AND), to trigger two envelopes on a higher voice panned left and a lower voice panned right; size then sets the odds of left vs right and they never fire together. Modulate size with a slow LFO and add clock feedback for a generative patch. Maps to Polyrhythm Studio as per-step random gating lanes.

skills.name: Lydian ambient soundscape layered by frequency range: lower-mid choir chords, mid noise-loop pad, dark saw bass and upper-mid granular/reversed piano sparkles, each checked with a mute test, then arranged by fade-ins, slowly opening filters and an automated reverb mix that merges everything into a cloud
skills.goal: Build a lush ambient soundscape at 70 BPM in a Lydian key by assigning each layer a frequency range rather than stacking similar pads. Write a 16-bar extended-chord cadence (Cmaj7 → Cadd#11 with the #11 a semitone from the 5th an octave down for gentle dissonance → back to C with the 9th), voice it on a soft choir, bounce it, then filter + EQ + big convolution reverb (lower mids). Add a mid pad: single noise-loop oscillator, soft attack and release, lowpass, a sparser two-note voicing of the same changes an octave up, a slow wandering LFO on noise rate/fade, slight detune spread, tube saturation whose drive is modulated by random noise, a phaser for wash and a huge reverb. Add a dark warm bass (two saws, gradually opening envelope, noise-modulated saturation, chorus, lowpass). Cover the upper mids/highs with a looped granular piano one-shot (small scan, mid grain size, EQ, echo) playing chord tones, bounced and reversed for reverse hits through a big boost EQ, echo and a very large reverb, plus a textured sample through the same chain. Mute-test every layer; keep only the ones you can still hear adding something. Arrange as a slow-evolving piece: bounce layers to audio, fade the intro in, sprinkle unreversed sparkles, slowly open each layer's lowpass over the whole track, and automate the reverb mix on the reversed layer from dry-ish to fully wet so it ends as a sparkly cloud. Polyrhythm Studio: per-layer band roles + long filter/reverb-mix control lanes.

skills.name: Ambient 44-bar arrangement map: low pad + light percussion, high pad at bar 5, piano at bar 13, shaker at ~bar 17, a mid-track strip-back to shaker/hat that sets up a return with new piano chords, and a coda that ends on the piano
skills.goal: Turn a 4-5 bar ambient loop into a ~44-bar song with a deliberate shape: set the tone with a low pad and sparse rim/cymbal (bars 1-5), add a high pad at bar 5 for gentle rising action, add piano around bar 13 and shaker around bar 16-17 to reach the 'full track', then strip the main percussion and low pad (keep only shaker and hat) for about 8 bars so the ending feels near, bring everything back around bar 33 with piano chords the listener has not heard yet (the spike of interest), stop the percussion half a bar early and end on the calming piano chords at bar 45 as a coda. Voice the new chords so the low pad only plays the notes that change while the piano replays the full chord every bar.

skills.name: Ambient/electronic multi-section arrangement: open with layered textures for drama, ground with a short bass hit, signal each new section with a small auditory cue (hat, whoosh, snare), change tempo per section, then a final push and a taper-out
skills.goal: Arrange a long ambient/electronic piece as several bite-sized sections that each lead the listener on. Open by drawing the listener in with layered high-frequency textures (modulated square-wave glitches resampled and glitched again, pads on top) to build drama; ground it with a simple four-bar bass 'boom'; go to a first big drop around bar 56 where a whoosh/boom sample and sidechained bass start. Signal each section change with a small cue that tells the listener change is coming (tiny hats entering, a whoosh, a snare), but skip the cue when the incoming part is soft enough to stand alone. Change section tempo/key via a master tempo lane (about 131 BPM to 111 to 136 in the source). Give each element space to breathe and let them live inside one another. Finish with a 'final push' (hat in, bass line changes, one pad ducked 4-5 dB to make space), then taper: bass fades out, leaving the inner atmosphere.

skills.name: Eight-bar build-up template: seven bars of risers, drums and sustained parts, one bar of pre-drop with everything cut, low end automated away, kick doubling schedule, filtered-in snare, single-note pad with pitch rise, and a readable vocal before the drop
skills.goal: Build a 4/4 build-up before a drop. Structure: 8 bars (16 bars for drum and bass). Seven bars of risers, drums and sustained instruments; the final bar is the pre-drop where everything else cuts off (snare roll, pre-drop vocal, sub build). Transitions: into the build-up use quiet up-risers and down-filters starting at its first bar; take one note of a chord-progression pad, hold it for the build, and automate pitch up over the last four bars; use vocals that actually say something in the last four bars (chop only the first four); thin the drums before the build if there is no breakdown, filter them in gradually if there is. Into the drop: always include one pre-drop bar, gradually automate low end out of bass, pads and risers, and optionally dip the loudest elements (not vocals) just before the drop. Elements: kick every beat for 4 bars, doubled for 2, doubled again for 1 (and through the last bar if the vocal matches), filtering out as it goes; a snare every step, filtering in from already half-open, plus a second low snare after 4 bars; hats/claps/percussion loop for depth; bring back an element from the intro/breakdown as a sustained part with a riser; layer multiple quiet risers.

skills.name: Breakdown arrangement after a drop: 4-bar break of impacts and reverse sweeps, two 8-bar breakdown halves (chords from the drop with rhythm removed, melody simplified then foreshadowed through a rising lowpass), then an 8-bar build-up of chopped parts and one silent bar before the drop
skills.goal: Lay out the section after a drop with markers: Break (4 bars) → Breakdown 1 (8) → Breakdown 2 (8) → Build-up (8) → drop. Break: big impact, sub drop, reverse crashes/sweeps and a quiet ambience bed. Breakdown effects first: repeat impacts and sub drops at each breakdown start, add a quiet background-motion loop and shaker with lots of reverb and low dry level. Breakdown harmony: copy the chords from the drop, remove the rhythm and merge notes into long chords, and simplify offbeat notes. Layer a soft piano with a second synth, and add automation (volume or cutoff rising at the end of each repetition) for reverse-like tension; make a reverse piano by recording a hit and reversing it. Melody: use the drop melody simplified (first four notes, rest, next five). Breakdown 2: same material plus 'drop clap' accents with reverb to signal the second half, a simple piano melody, and the full drop melody low-pass filtered in with an automation ramp from closed to open. Build-up: chop breakdown sounds down to the first chord repeated, chop more in the second half, add up-filters, reverse sweeps/impacts at the start, a snare fill (4 hits then doubled), melody foreshadowed with its ending in the last bar, then everything cut one bar before the drop.

skills.name: Ambient chord arrangement: give each chord tone to a separate instrument (sub root, synth third a tenth up, choir fifth, string doubling the third), each swelling in on its own, moving in parallel and spread wide, at about 55 BPM
skills.goal: Make a 2-3 chord ambient progression feel like a living choir. Use a slow tempo around 55 BPM (6 s breath cycle) or 60 BPM / halftime. Split each triad across instruments instead of block chords: a sub plays the root of each chord and swells with the mod wheel; a dark synth pad plays the third an octave and more up (a tenth), a choir-like pad adds the fifth above, and a frozen string reinforces the third to define the key. Each part swells in at its own pace and the voices move in parallel. Spread notes apart (avoid close block voicing in the low register to avoid mud): move the third up an octave, the fifth up an octave, or the fifth above the third. Then add reverse textures that move within the key.

skills.name: Emotional cinematic arrangement arc: background-only subtle intro, gradual additions, a climax built first where the melody appears, gentle fade outro, melody derived from chord arpeggios, light master chain
skills.goal: Build a warm, nostalgic cinematic piece around a familiar chord progression played by piano, strings, choir, bells/celesta and harp. Arc: start from a very subtle, transparent warmth that appears from nowhere; keep a background with no certain melody; add instruments little by little; one-note tremolo 'angelic wind' swell from a soft lead with volume automation (octave-up double); a climax where all emotion and melody goes (you can write it first and build the other parts around it); strings that fade vibrato in rather than starting vibrating immediately; an outro that fades continuously to nowhere with a final legato fade and a single-note cymbal swell. Melody method: write the chord progression, arpeggiate chord notes forward/backward on piano, loop ~10 rounds, then edit notes.

skills.name: Per-element sidechain shapes: bass ducks the whole kick, mids/highs duck only the punch, depth set by loudness, multiband for full-range sounds
skills.goal: Set sidechain ducking per element instead of one kick-shaped duck on everything: the bass and low end duck deeply for the whole kick length (returning exactly as the tail ends), mid/high instruments duck only briefly around the kick's punch/transient, and loud foreground layers duck deeper than quiet background layers. Full-range sounds such as a reese use multiband sidechain with separate low and mid/high shapes. Don't fix pumping by lowering the mix knob, because partial ducking leaves kick and element overlapping and that shared volume hits the master limiter early. Delta vs the generic sidechain-compressor-duck-synth-pads skill: shape and depth rules per element and the loudness/limiter reason.

skills.name: EQ for balance in three questions: what is the focus, is the clash static or dynamic (sidechained dynamic EQ), and where in the stereo field (mid-only)
skills.goal: Resolve frequency competition between a focus element (for example a lead vocal) and other loud parts (lead synth, mid bass, piano) with a three-question framework instead of a fixed EQ scoop. (1) Name the section's focus and which parts still compete with it. (2) If the overlap changes with the focus's level, notes and pauses, use a dynamic EQ on the competing part with the focus as its sidechain key, so cuts follow the focus. (3) If the focus is mono but the competitor is stereo, run that dynamic EQ in mid-only mode so the sides keep their full level. Delta vs generic sidechain/EQ skills: the decision order and the mid-only dynamic cut.

skills.name: Eight-bar rhythmic phrasing: spine beat on strong beats, bar-level A/B/A/C variation, and a last-bar D that is either a fill (adds syncopation and toms) or an empty (drops the kick or main rhythm) to set up the next section
skills.goal: Turn a one-bar loop into an 8-bar phrase that tells the listener where the section boundaries are. Build a spine beat (kick on 1-2-3-4, snare/clap on the backbeat 2 and 4, closed hat on the offbeat 'ands'), then put lighter percussion on the weak 16ths ('e' and 'a'), mixing low-mid and high sounds there. Use bar-level variation: A = core bar, B = one small change (add, remove or swap one hit), back to A in bar 3, C = a slightly bigger change at bar 4, then A material again, and D in bar 8: either a fill (extra syncopation, snare hits on weak beats, extra eighth-note kicks, toms high to low) or an empty (remove most or all main rhythmic elements, e.g. drop the kick for the last bar) before the next downbeat. The bigger the coming change, the more anticipation the fill or empty should build. Optionally layer a polymeter (for example a 3-step pattern over a 4-beat grid) so loops shift against each other over time.

skills.name: Rule of three for repeating musical ideas: play a 4-bar idea twice so it sticks, then on the third pass either go somewhere new (new melody on the same chords, or new chords) or start the same and diverge halfway
skills.goal: Stop over-looping a phrase. Play a musical idea (e.g. a 4-bar chord progression with melody) once to spark interest and a second time to reinforce it so the listener can remember it. On the third pass, never repeat it unchanged: option 1, go somewhere different (a new melody over the same chords, or a new progression with a new melody); option 2, start the third pass the same and diverge partway (around halfway through the phrase). Choose the option by intent (the response you want from the listener). Use as a check across a loop-based arrangement.

skills.name: Section transition toolkit: layered risers and impacts, throwing a part to a growing delay, a next-section instrument entering early, stacked exponential automation, resampled or reverse-reverb whooshes, removing elements or silence, and transitions that cross or hang over the bar line
skills.goal: Glue song sections together so they don't feel like 'one thing, then the next thing'. Add transition sounds (risers, whooshes, downlifters; layer and vary them by intensity so they aren't the same every time; synthesize them for control), plus an impact on the landing downbeat (crash or noisy hit into reverb). Make transitions out of existing parts: play the transition (pull back or push harder), throw a vocal or lead into a delay whose mix goes 0 to 100% while feedback grows and a resonant filter sweeps, add upward multiband compression for excitement, and let an instrument from the next section enter early with a pickup. Stack several automations at once (distortion drive, width, delay or grain mix, filter cutoff, envelope decay and release from plucky to ringing) and compensate output gain. Design the end sound first, then automate toward it. Shape curves (exponential by default; hold-then-ramp; turn-back; slam-then-recede). Resample parts and time-stretch or pitch them into custom whooshes; reverse a fully-wet reverb print before the hit. Remove sounds: cut drums or bass, or use a moment of silence. Let transitions cross the bar line (drop instruments for the first beat of the new section) or hang over and fade into it. Combine techniques.

skills.name: Slow ambient harmony in one key: suspended and 7sus4 chords, a held root under a changing upper chord, or a static chord over a moving bass note, plus inversions and a band-passed 1-2-3 scale-degree cluster for tension, all moved slowly over a long timeline
skills.goal: Get movement in a long-form ambient or drone track without leaving the key. Pick one key (a minor or modal key such as Aeolian, Dorian or Lydian suits dark, suspended moods) and stay in it for the whole track; a key change should signal a completely new passage. Use 2-4-note chords: sus2 (1-2-5) or sus4 (1-4-5) over a low root as neutral, suspended openers, then the minor triad, then a 7sus-style shape (1-5-7) for contrast. Create variation from the same notes: invert (put a different chord tone on the bottom), drop notes down an octave or two, or make a non-root chord tone the root of the next chord. Two core motion techniques: (1) keep the root as a pedal and change the upper chord above it (e.g. A root under Am, Dm, C); (2) keep the upper chord static and move the bass note under it (e.g. Am over the 6th degree). For tension, play scale degrees 1-2-3 together as a cluster and squeeze it with a high-pass and low-pass to roughly 600-1000 Hz. Spread single chord tones across several layered instruments instead of one dense patch. Make changes slowly across the timeline.

skills.name: Cinematic taiko-style ensemble drums from white noise: velocity sets the amp and filter decay, a resonant 60 Hz high-pass plus low boost adds weight, a tanh soft clip and limiter go before a large-hall convolution reverb, with optional detuned sine, FM sub and round-robin sample layers
skills.goal: Make big cinematic ensemble drums (taiko-like) with no recordings, using any synth with a noise oscillator, a filter, two envelopes and velocity sensitivity. Think in four categories: frequency, amplitude, time and timbre. Start with white noise; amp envelope with no sustain and a short decay, with velocity routed to decay (soft hits short, hard hits long and ringing) and a wide velocity-to-level range. Add a low-pass filter (about 1 kHz) with its own short envelope on cutoff, also scaled by velocity, so each hit starts bright and closes darker; add a little filter drive. EQ: resonant high-pass at about 60 Hz plus a low bell boost for weight, a mud cut, presence, a slight high shelf; add a little release so hits breathe. Soft clip (tanh waveshaper) driven a little by that low boost to mimic an overloaded ensemble, trim the output and the extreme sub. Put a limiter or maximizer, then a convolution reverb with a cathedral or large-hall impulse (shortened, low end tamed, highs damped, about 5 kHz lifted). Layers: several detuned sines with a pitch envelope for tone, an FM sub at 20-50 Hz, and a round-robin layer of rattly found-object hits with slight random pitch to avoid machine-gunning.

skills.name: Make a weak drum (e.g. a clap) cut through and drive the groove with band-passed overdrive: choose the band that gets distorted, push the drive too far then back off, use tone to tame harsh top, set the dynamics control low for a tight punch, blend dry/wet, and level-match
skills.goal: Fix a drum hit that sounds wimpy or sits on top of the mix. On the soloed hit (reverb off, low cut kept so it doesn't fight the kick and bass), insert an overdrive with a band-pass before the distortion stage, inside a group with a gain utility after it for level matching. Sweep the band-pass to find the range you want to emphasize (avoid the thick, murky lows) and narrow the Q roughly. Push the drive hard to hear what it does, then back it off (about 60%) so the brittle upper-mid hiss doesn't dominate. Use the tone control as a top-end cut. Set the dynamics control lower for a tighter, punchier, shorter-feeling hit, or higher for a washed-out, relaxed one (it acts like note length and articulation for the groove). Dial dry/wet (parallel) from about 50 to 100%. Level-match against bypass with the gain utility, then put the reverb back and fine-tune in context, leaving final tweaks for the mixdown.

skills.name: High-pass phaser chord pad: saw chords through a heavily resonant high-pass whose cutoff is automated, ping-pong 1/4 delay and a big reverb both low-cut at about 200 Hz, a phaser on a slow 2-bar cycle, a harmonizer shifted to the 3rd harmonic for a bell tone, unison and light compression
skills.goal: Make moving chords or a pad from a plain saw wave using a high-pass filter and a phaser (works in any synth with these, or as post-processing on a saw). Play low chords on a single saw. Add a high-pass filter with resonance turned way up and automate its cutoff to sweep the chord's movement. Add a ping-pong delay at 1/4 note with a low cut around 200 Hz (so the bass isn't muddy) and some stereo spread, then a large reverb, also low-cut about 200 Hz, with size up, slightly longer decay, damping and wet up. Add a phaser set to complete one cycle every 2 bars (its direction sets whether it sweeps up or down) for slow top-end motion. Add a harmonizer (octave copies) with amount and width high, then shift its interval from the octave to the 3rd harmonic for a bell-like tone. Add unison voices to taste, light compression, and pull the highs and some mids down a little.

skills.name: Three-layer ambient starter in about 30 minutes: a slow-envelope wavetable pad with a 4-bar bipolar position LFO and random cutoff drift, a saw-plus-sine bass pad through a 24 dB low-pass, and a sustain-less detail voice whose filter is stepped by a sample-and-hold style modulator into heavy delay and reverb, all composed by frequency region
skills.goal: Build the core of an ambient track (70-80 BPM, one minor key, 32-bar canvas) from three complementary layers. Pad: wavetable osc with attack about 3-5 s (4 s), decay about 4 s, sustain a few dB down, long release; 5 unison voices with moderate detune; wavetable position on a bipolar LFO synced to 4 bars; low-pass cutoff set to the 'sweet spot' where partials just peek through, with a random (chaos) modulator on cutoff at a low depth; a sub osc one octave down kept quiet; a second wavetable osc routed around the filter at low level and auto-panned by a 2-bar LFO for width. Send (not insert) to a dotted-eighth dual delay and a very long room/hall reverb (about 55 s decay, 100% wet on the return). Write only a few sustained notes over 32 bars, then pull the cutoff down and let the reverb do the opening. Bass pad: faster envelope, saw through a 24 dB/oct low-pass plus a sine, a touch of reverb, one long root note. Detail voice: attack-decay envelope with zero sustain (a key that rises and falls regardless of hold), 24 dB low-pass whose cutoff is moved by a stepped random (sample-and-hold) modulator at a slow rate, cranked delay and reverb. Check the layers on a spectrum analyser and place each in a different frequency region.

skills.name: Design four bass types from scratch with fit-to-kick rules: a punchy 808 (sine, hold and 1.5 s decay, a 35 ms pitch-envelope punch, tube drive, low boost, attack delayed 80-100 ms when the kick already punches), a pluck bass (mono square through an enveloped 24 dB low-pass plus a wide unison top layer), a sidechained saw growl, and a click-free sine sub
skills.goal: Four punchy bass recipes. 808: one sine osc, attack near 0 (raise slightly until the click disappears), hold about 300-400 ms, decay about 1.5 s, sustain 0; a little wavetable bend/warp for character; a second envelope (attack about 0.5 ms, hold 0, decay about 35 ms, sustain 0, release about 15 ms) routed to master tune for a kick-like pitch punch (set amount to the middle); tube distortion with mix pulled back; EQ lift around 100 Hz. If the kick already supplies the punch, raise the 808 attack to about 80-100 ms so it fills in behind the kick instead of sidechaining. Pluck/house bass: mono voice, square wave through a 24 dB low-pass, short attack, no hold, low sustain, some release; the same envelope also drives cutoff for the pluck; drive the filter a little; add a second osc (PWM-type wave, 5-7 unison voices, detuned) for a wide top, keep content below about 100-150 Hz mono, reverb and delay with low cut. Growl bass: saw with a low-pass, second osc with 7-8 unison voices, mono, very short release, an LFO shaped as a sidechain duck on both osc levels, cutoff on a macro, then boost about 140 Hz to keep it a bass. Sub: sine, one voice, mono/legato, attack about 5 ms and a short release to avoid clicks.

skills.name: Make synth layers read as strings or orchestra by obscuring them: two saw-based arpeggiated plucks moving in opposite directions, a fast-open filter envelope and vibrato, a shared pitch-shifting modulated reverb, and level automation plus sidechain so the listener only hears brief glimpses without context
skills.goal: Imply acoustic strings with simple synthesis plus psychoacoustics. Harmonic content: saw-like spectra (strings and brass are close to a saw series). Layer two arpeggiators playing the same chords: one rising, one reversed so they cross; double the arp step time (half speed); each voice uses a brass-like filter envelope (opens fast, decays: a smoothed pluck), light unison, real vibrato, and a spectral/frequency-mode phaser masked to act above the fundamental so the note pitch stays clean; the second voice has a longer pluck, darker filter and more unison. Arp cycle length depends on chord note count, so voice chords deliberately. Send both to one shared reverb with large size and diffusion, low feedback, a downward pitch shimmer and high modulation depth. Then automate the layer's level by feel so it only comes through at chosen moments, and sidechain it under the drums; a supporting soft chord stack gets a big reverb with a gate so tails don't run on. The brain fills in an orchestra because it never hears the sound's before/after context.

skills.name: Loop-to-track arrangement where the finished loop is the climax and everything before it 'gives away' that loop gradually: whole elements, the power of elements (high-passed kick, thin high-and-low-passed bass), and the chord progression itself (root-note pedal first), with a change at every 8-bar boundary and an outro that mirrors the intro
skills.goal: Arrange a finished loop into a full track. First map a reference track: listen through and drop markers for what enters or leaves at each section (every 8 bars something changes). Treat your loop as the climax and plan how to reach it by giving things away over time. Drums first: copy the full drum loop to the start, high-pass the kick at about 120 Hz for the first 16 bars, start with fewer parts (no shaker/hats), bring shaker in, save hats and snare for later, and remove the kick's last bar (or last two bars) before each full-kick entry or drop. Atmosphere runs throughout. Bass: start as a single root-note pedal (monotonic) instead of the progression, with an octave jump at the end of each 8 bars; give away its power with labelled high-pass and low-pass filters automated from thin and dark to full. Melodic parts: bring in stripped-back fragments (first bar only, fewer notes), filter elements in instead of hard entries, reveal the full chord progression and full lead later; hold back some parts for the second drop. Outro: do the opposite of the intro (high-pass the kick again for 8 bars, filter the bass out and darker, return to the root pedal and a resolving last note).

skills.name: Turn a few played notes into a self-sustaining shimmering pad by feeding them once into a clean stereo delay at 99% feedback with very different left/right times (about 1 s and 150 ms), so the melody dissolves into a continuous texture for the rest of the track
skills.goal: Feedback-delay pad generator. Play a short phrase of three or four notes once into a neutral (uncoloured) stereo delay; nothing else is fed in for the rest of the track. Set feedback to the maximum safe value (99%) and set the delay times far apart: about 1 s on the left and about 150 ms on the right. The repeats keep cycling through the whole track; the original melody vanishes and is replaced by a shimmering secondary texture. Optional: use a tape-style delay instead for pitch warble, which strengthens the shimmer. Use the plain feedback control rather than cross-feed, which grows the signal quickly.

skills.name: Four levels of loop-to-story arrangement: (1) subtractive Lego-block arrangement from a duplicated loop shaped by an energy contour, (2) turnaround-and-marker transitions at section edges, (3) a performed protagonist element that crescendos and decrescendos across sections, (4) an additive cinematic pass that starts from silence and adds only motivated elements
skills.goal: Turn a 16-bar loop into a musical story in four escalating levels. Level 1 (subtractive): duplicate the loop across the whole target length (4-5 minutes), then cut away in 8- or 16-bar blocks following an energy contour (low start, build to the middle, kick-out dips, peak, outro); add a little silence at the start and room at the end for reverb tails. Level 2 (transitions): at each section edge add a turnaround (signals the end: remove low energy, reverse reverb swell or noise riser) and a marker on the downbeat (a splash: white noise, crash, one percussion hit into big reverb, stutter or false drop), built from the track's own timbres resampled, reversed or processed; transitions can be explicit or hypnotic. Level 3 (performance): record a performed element (e.g. filter, level or intensity moves on one sound) that starts mellow, grows to dominant and subsides, spanning section boundaries as the 'protagonist'; split and move the audio if needed. Level 4 (additive): start from silence and add elements only when the music is motivated (when you would get bored), like a film composer, letting well-designed elements play for a long time.

skills.name: Synthesize a whole drum kit (808, kick, clap, snare, closed and open hat) from a basic synth: sine and noise sources, envelope-drawn transients, fast pitch envelopes, and targeted EQ, then test and re-tweak each sound inside a real beat
skills.goal: Build six drum sounds in one synth with no samples. 808: sine tuned so its fundamental sits around 45 Hz (an octave below where it first lands), plus a saw and white noise whose levels follow a drawn envelope with a quick dip for the transient; low-pass the saw; boost mids a little, soft-clip, use a very gentle high-pass around 20 Hz (a steep one sounds bad), and a narrow bell cut around 78 Hz; optional parallel copy with reverb faded in and kept to the sides. Kick: sine pitched down, very short amp envelope, a very fast pitch envelope (about 0.07 s) on pitch, soft clip, light bit-crush, multiband drive, cut boxy mids around 400 Hz, high-pass. Clap: white noise whose level envelope has three quick transients then one longer decay (about 0.085 s spacing on a 9-step grid), band-limited (energy above about 600 Hz, key areas about 1 kHz and 6 kHz), high end added with bells not shelves, a little chorus and very short delays for width, compression, reduce side highs. Snare: two or three sines in octaves (the reference showed tones at about 240, 484 and 1 kHz), noise with two quick transients, one shared filter, a very short pitch envelope on all tones, distortion; optionally layer the clap. Closed hat: white noise, about 0.22 s envelope, band/high-pass that keeps some mids. Open hat: longer noise envelope with a second transient, low-cut reverb, very short (1/64) ping-pong delay, shorten decay to taste. Render each and tweak inside a beat (e.g. re-export pitched up a few semitones).
